key_insight: Introducing an anchoring mechanism (a shared reference/penalty) lets independently trained predictors dramatically reduce their expected squared prediction disagreement; disagreement can be driven to (near) zero by tuning natural training parameters like anchor strength and sample size.
problem_solved: How to control and certify model disagreement — the expected squared difference in predictions between two models trained on independent data without coordinating training — so models behave consistently across training runs and datasets.
method: Define model disagreement as the expected squared difference in predictions between two independently trained models.
Add an anchoring component to the training objective (a penalty or constraint that pulls model predictions toward a common anchor/predictor or reference estimator).

Provide theoretical bounds and empirical evaluation showing disagreement decreases as a function of anchor strength and data/sample parameters, without requiring coordination between training processes.
impact: Practitioners get a simple, tuneable way to make models more consistent and reproducible across independent trainings, improving reliability for deployment, audits, and downstream decision-making while preserving standard training workflows.
visual_elements: Schematic: two training pipelines fed independent data that both connect to a common 'anchor' node, illustrating the anchoring penalty.
Line chart: disagreement (expected squared difference) on the y-axis vs anchor strength and/or sample size on the x-axis, showing decline to near zero.
Heatmap or scatter of prediction differences across input space before vs after anchoring to show reduced variance in outputs.
Icon set: anchor symbol (stability), twin-model silhouettes (agreement), and theoretical bound formula snippet (rigor).
paper_authors: Eric Eaton, Surbhi Goel, Marcel Hussing, Michael Kearns, Aaron Roth
